patient_information: The patient is a 14-year-old boy from rural Malawi.
chief_complaint: The patient presented to a local hospital with an extensive necrotic wound on his right foot, three weeks after being bitten by a snake.
history_of_present_illness: Three weeks prior to presentation, the patient was bitten by a snake while playing. Shortly after the bite, he developed haemorrhagic bullae on his right leg, his gums started to bleed, and he vomited extensively. He was initially taken to a traditional healer, after which the bleeding and vomiting settled. However, he subsequently developed intense pain and swelling at the site of the bite, which progressed to the necrotic wound seen on admission.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from rural Malawi and was bitten on a path leading through rocky grassland to his family's maize field. The snake was described as brown with V-shaped black bands on its back, approximately one metre long, and it hissed loudly before biting. This description is consistent with an African puff-adder (Bitis arietans).
vitals: On admission, the patient appeared weak and was in respiratory distress. His temperature was 39.4°C, pulse was 126 bpm, blood pressure was 85/60 mmHg, and respiratory rate was 30 breaths per minute.
physical_exam: There was an extensive, foul-smelling necrosis affecting his right foot and ankle, with exposed tendons. The right lower leg was swollen, and he was unable to bend his right ankle. The inguinal lymph nodes were enlarged on the right side. His urine was clear, a rectal exam showed no signs of bleeding, there was no haemoptysis upon provoked coughing, and fundoscopy was normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: The 20-minute whole blood clotting test (WBCT20) was normal. Blood tests showed a haemoglobin of 9.5 mg/dL (reference 12–14) and potassium (K+) of 4.2 mmol/L. The WBC and platelet counts were not specified in the provided table.
differential_diagnosis: The primary diagnostic challenge was identifying the snake species. The African puff-adder (Bitis arietans) was considered the most likely cause due to the snake's described appearance (one metre long, V-pattern on back), aggressive behavior (hissing), and the clinical syndrome of massive local swelling, haemorrhagic bullae, extensive necrosis, and systemic haemorrhage. The saw-scaled viper (Echis species) can produce similar symptoms. Bites by mambas were considered less likely as they are relatively uncommon.
management_and_clinical_course: Due to the three-week delay, antivenom was not administered. The patient was diagnosed as septic and managed with broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and 'ventilatory support'. He also received tetanus prophylaxis. The wound required surgical management with several debridements, followed by successful mesh-grafting. He was discharged several weeks later with some residual functional impairment of his right foot, requiring outpatient physiotherapy.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was a severe cytotoxic and haematotoxic snake envenomation with delayed presentation, complicated by extensive tissue necrosis and sepsis. The causative agent was most probably an African puff-adder (Bitis arietans), a conclusion based on the eyewitness description of the snake, the geographic location, and the clinical evolution characterized by initial systemic haemorrhage (bleeding gums) and severe, progressive local effects (haemorrhagic bullae, swelling, and deep necrosis).
